title: US country music star Ella Langley cancels show due to 'security threat'
content: US country music star Ella Langley has said she had to cancel her sold-out concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma on Friday night, due to a "serious security threat". The singer made what she called the "incredibly difficult" decision around two hours before the show at the 19,000-seater arena was due to start. In a post on Instagram, the 27-year-old said the threat involved "the safety of my fans, the venue staff and my team". Cpt Richard Meulenberg from Tulsa Police Department said a person had called saying "great harm" would be done at the event with "shots fired and bombs." He stated his team had checked the venue at BOK Center several times before the show and "could not find any threat". "The event was ready to go," he added, saying officers with sniffer dogs did a sweep of the arena again after the phone call was made. "We could not find a credible threat," he said, stressing that the person who had made the call "disrupted this entire event" for thousands of Langley fans. The star - who did not give any further details - also apologised to her fans, saying additional information regarding ticket refunds "will be shared as soon as possible". BOK Center issued its own statement, saying that "the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. "We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologise to fans who planned to attend." In September, Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas overtook Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history. Its success helped the singer from Alabama to sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May. Isaias is continuing across the Southeastern US after being downgraded from a hurricane to a post-tropical cyclone. Youth group Bree, is marking 20 years with a two-day music and dance workshop at half term. The Pentagon says the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, but experts suggest officials are reading the country wrong. The US president told a rally he had "never heard of" the winner, former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay. title: Meet India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi
content: When India's Gen Z-led protesters return to Delhi this weekend for demonstrations seeking the resignation of the country's top election official, one of the prominent faces at the forefront will be that of a 29-year-old PhD student. Neha Bora is a theatre artist and activist who has been with the All India Students' Association (Aisa), a Left-wing organisation known for campus politics, for the past decade and been its president for the past two years. But Neha's - who uses "they" and "them" as personal pronouns - visibility is no longer limited to campuses. Viral videos over the past few days show them being dragged through the street by a group of female police officials, climbing on top of police barricades, raising their fist and shouting slogans, and being detained. Photos of them smiling while being carried away by policewomen have also gone viral. In a recent BBC Bangla interview , Neha played down the attention they've been receiving. "I know it happened in front of the camera so it seems like it's something different," they said. "But I have seen all student activists with the Left doing the same things that I have been doing. It's just that there is a camera on me, so people think something different is happening." The attention on Neha comes at a time when several high-profile protests are being held on India's streets in what is being seen as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power. There's the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a Gen Z-led online satirical movement - that held weeks-long protests in Delhi in the summer over education reforms. It ended in July only after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. Separately, some of India's opposition parties, especially the Congress, have also taken to the streets over electoral reforms. For the past few days, videos of Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra being shoved and jostled and detained have gone viral and made headlines in India. Saturday's protest in Delhi has been called by the CJP, which is seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating electoral rolls to favour Modi's BJP. Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the accusation. Although not a member of the CJP, Neha has said their group would also participate. Born in the northern state of Uttarakhand, Neha lived in different cities as a child as their army officer father moved for his postings. After graduating from Delhi University, they did a master's degree from Ambedkar University in the capital and are now a PhD student at the prestigious Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). Neha first came into the spotlight in the summer during the CJP's protest over education reforms. Neha and Aisa were at the protest from the start, but not many knew them at that point. That changed after 28 June, when educationist and scientist Sonam Wangchuk began a hunger strike in CJP's support and Neha and a few others from Aisa also joined him. "It was an obvious choice for us. We've been protesting against paper leaks and education reforms for a long time," Neha later said in an interview. While most of the attention was focused on Wangchuk, whose reputation and presence galvanised the movement, Neha's outspokenness and combative speeches began to get them noticed. After Wangchuk and others were moved to hospital , Neha continued fasting despite having lost 8kg. Even after being moved to hospital, they said in a video: "The fight continues. Once I've recovered, we'll meet you again on the streets to continue our fight for our right." After the protests ended in July, Neha has established themselves as a Gen Z leader who's courted by the CJP and media, besides appearing alongside Rahul Gandhi at press conferences. But Neha's involvement with Aisa and leftist politics and statements criticising PM Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and other BJP leaders have also led to "lots of disagreements with my family as my parents are staunch supporters of BJP". And last month, at least three police complaints were lodged in Uttar Pradesh state by BJP against Neha for making "objectionable remarks" against the chief minister - they came two days after Aisa's police complaint that Neha had received death threats . Neha, who has been travelling to many Indian cities to participate in protests in support of students, also made headlines when a man allegedly threw ink at them during a protest march in Jharkhand state. A photo Neha shared on Instagram showed their face streaked with ink stains. Police said they had detained the man. The noisy protests and repeated detentions have earned Neha a reputation for being a street fighter. "The streets have always dictated the course of politics in this country and they will continue to do so, more so in the coming few years," they told BBC Bangla. "If we look at the social changes of the recent past, those social changes did not come from people sitting in parliament; they came from the streets," they said. Now as the authorities gear up for 10 October's protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Kumar, Neha and Aisa have said they would be back in the streets with the CJP to "protect democracy". We explain why Indonesia’s peatland fires are so difficult to battle and produce so much haze. Known for his intense performances, Patekar carved out a distinctive place in Indian cinema. It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul. Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani had been secretly released on parole in 2025, after serving less than half his sentence. The skipper who led India to the historic 2025 World Cup win has stepped down from her role in all three formats. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Three men found guilty of murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico
content: Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024. The men's full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús. They are yet to be sentenced - but are likely to spend the rest of their lives in a prison. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them". During the trial in the northern Baja California state, the court heard that the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area. Their bodies were later found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads. The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico. Debra Robinson and her husband Martin have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial, and delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments before Friday's verdict. "It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin said. Family members of Carter Rhoad joined the trial by video link. Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us". During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants. In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo alias "El Kekas", was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery. At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings. The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico. The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time. Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them. At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to honour the men by paddling out at a popular surfing spot and throwing flowers into the sea. Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California. Amid the demands for action, state Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence. "Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said. "I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time." The Pentagon says the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, but experts suggest officials are reading the country wrong. The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general also alleges the co-pilot was trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport. The US president told a rally he had "never heard of" the winner, former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay. The planned firing-squad execution on 3 December has led to questions about legality and purpose. Police say they checked the concert venue in Tulsa, Oklahoma but "could not find any threat". title: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
content: Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate. The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening. Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas. Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean. Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm. In Florida, those evacuations include coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!" Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm. Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific. It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October. The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned. After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday. As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km). The Florida Panhandle and the rest of the US Gulf Coast are facing fierce winds and heavy rain as the hurricane barrels down. There is also the potential for accompanying tornadoes, Melissa Watson, a Florida-based meteorologist at the National Weather Service told the BBC. For those who have not evacuated, "the main thing will be having multiple ways to receive warnings" about tornadoes and storm surges, Watson said. "If you are near the coast, being able to move to higher ground," is also essential in the event of storm surges. "We want people to be safe, so don't go out there trying to look for damage ... to post on social media," she added. "We want people to remain inside and safe while the hurricane is moving through." Even before the storm made landfall, hundreds of thousands were without power in the country's southeast - and Alabama, Florida and Georgia have issued states of emergency as they brace for heavy rains and flooding. More than 350,000 were in the dark in Florida and another 170,000 in Alabama saw outages, according to PowerOutage.us. The hurricane's winds are expected to be felt further inland in Georgia, albeit at a lesser intensity, where already about 8,000 customers were without power. People on the coast of the Florida panhandle have been told to seek immediate shelter under an "Extreme Wind Warning". Some Florida officials have ordered residents to "Get out NOW!", urging people to follow evacuation orders. John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left. "It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said. "Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said, Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over". A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes". Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home. People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this". One indicator of a storm's severity to communities in the southern US is whether the stalwart restaurant chain The Waffle House would close its doors to customers. On Friday, it did. A Waffle House spokesperson confirmed to the BBC that the chain had already closed a number of locations in the hurricane's path and "will continue monitoring conditions". US President Donald Trump said he will no longer attend a major American football college game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama because of the hurricane, shifting plans to attend a rally in Tennessee instead. Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend. Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters. Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific. While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California. Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide. Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides". It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding. With additional reporting by Simon King. The Pentagon says the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, but experts suggest officials are reading the country wrong. The US president told a rally he had "never heard of" the winner, former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay. The planned firing-squad execution on 3 December has led to questions about legality and purpose. Police say they checked the concert venue in Tulsa, Oklahoma but "could not find any threat". title: Queen reflects on reading 'forbidden' Lady Chatterley's Lover under the pillow
content: Queen Camilla has recalled secretly reading Lady Chatterley's Lover, the passionate and controversial novel by DH Lawrence, as a teenager in the 1960s. "As teenagers you read a lot of romances. It was the moment of Lady Chatterley, under our pillows, reading that by torchlight. You know the minute something is forbidden, you want to get hold of it," she said about the novel that had been at the centre of an obscenity trial. The Queen spoke about memorable moments in her own reading for BBC documentary The Book That Changed My Life, and about the life-changing power of literacy and books. She gave a glimpse of how regular reading is part of her royal marriage: "It's like the best tonic in the world. My husband and I actually read before dinner, just sitting quietly and reading. "He loves biographies, and PG Wodehouse. I occasionally, when I'm deep in a book, hear him roaring with laughter about something," said the Queen about the King's affection for the author of the Jeeves and Wooster comic novels. "It's very off-putting, I can't get back into my book, or I'll suddenly start weeping. But it's a lovely, quiet time. I think it would be a complete and utter tragedy if books went forever," she said. The Queen also revealed more of her own youthful reading, saying she was "mesmerised" by Charles Dickens's Tale of Two Cities and its depiction of those watching the guillotine during the French Revolution. "Those ghastly women sitting there knitting while everybody had their heads chopped off," she said. The Queen, who is 79 years old, said she was part of a generation of women who missed out on higher education, which made reading and books even more important. "I left school quite young. In my day, women didn't go to university, so I think reading has been most of my education," she said. The documentary shows the impact of reading on people in stressful circumstances - and that includes Omar, who discovered a love of reading while in prison. Reading was a way of escaping the confines of a cell, at least in his imagination - and the book he remembers most was a tattered copy of Jack Higgins's war thriller, The Eagle Has Landed. Chatting to Omar after the screening of the documentary, he said that what struck him most about meeting the Queen was her "authenticity". He said that off camera she was genuinely interested in his role working in prison education - helping a prison population that's facing chronic levels of illiteracy. The pair also shared unexpected connections. Camilla's father, Bruce Shand, had also been a prisoner, in a different kind of captivity, as a prisoner of war captured in North Africa during the Second World War. He had used books as an emotional escape tunnel, during two and a half years of imprisonment. "He said he educated himself. He read every single book, from the Bible to the encyclopedia, whatever was there, he just sat there all day long and read and read. And I think that's how he survived it," said the Queen. She remembered how her father didn't want to talk about the war - "you bury it all because you've seen such horrendous things" - and so it was only when she read his memoir that she understood his experiences. "It was written from the heart. I mean, I cried through most of it. I found it so moving. Because if you think, I didn't know anything about it, and reading managed to get him through it." Omar said the Queen had recognised a connection. "She talked about the parallels, her father found reading in a prisoner of war camp. She definitely recognised the resemblance… being in a place you don't want to be and using books to escape it and then books elevating you on many levels," he said. Queen Camilla has been running her Queen's Reading Room project for five years, a kind of mega book club, with festivals and events and outreach projects, such as bringing books to homeless shelters. It's part of her campaign to promote and protect the value of reading and to stop us becoming a culture of screen addicts. Perhaps the most moving parts of the documentary are the stories of how books can become lifelines for people facing bereavement or intense loneliness. Ian, from the north-east of England, spoke with heartbreaking candour about finding himself in a state of complete social isolation after the death of his mother. "I used to sit with my head on the kitchen table, crying. It was such a difficult period of loneliness, of nothingness," he said. Reading and becoming part of a book group proved a lifesaver for him, coaxing him back to his own happy ending. There's a powerful testimony from Peter, a Merseyside truck driver, who had to admit that he wasn't able to read and needed help, after the shame of having to keep inventing excuses to his children who wanted a bedtime story. He was taught to read by an adult education project - and he proudly shows the copy of JK Rowling's Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone that has become his own stepping stone to literacy. Perhaps the most sobering statistic in this documentary is that there are eight million adults in the UK who struggle with even basic levels of literacy. Speaking after the screening, Big Issue founder John Bird blamed the scourge of adult illiteracy on a long-term political failure in tackling the "inheritance of poverty". "We did not educate the people who found education difficult - and I was one of them," he said, having learned to read as a youngster in prison. "People were written off, now we're paying for that," he added. On the Queen's literacy campaign, he said she provided an important symbolic focus. He likened it to how sales of the Big Issue increase when Prince William helps to sell the magazine for the homeless. "You don't have to be a monarchist to buy into this idea - I wouldn't say that I was a monarchist, but I do believe in the power of certain personalities to enable a lot of people to say I'm going to get stuck into this," said Lord Bird. "I think it's wonderful books change people's lives," said the Queen, having revealed some clues about how books have turned the pages of her own story. The Book That Changed My Life, BBC2, 14 October, 21.00 and iPlayer. Sign up here to get the latest royal stories and analysis every week with our Royal Watch newsletter. Those outside the UK can sign up here . Ian Kirby, from Gateshead, says joining a book group turned his life around after his mother's death. The bestselling author and former politician died on Monday at the age of 86. The King and Queen watched events including Highland dancing, caber tossing and pipe bands performing at the annual event in Royal Deeside. The eight-day visit will see the royal pair travel to Antigua before King Charles travels to the Bahamas and Guyana. title: Flydubai attacker began a 'drift towards extremism and terrorism' in Australia, UAE says
content: The Omani co-pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai plane started a "drift towards extremism and terrorism" while studying in Australia, United Arab Emirates officials say. UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi also alleged the pilot - widely named as Hamam al-Hammami - was last week trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport in a "suicide attack". He wounded the captain in the cockpit with the emergency crash axe before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew on the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight was able to land the aircraft in Saudi Arabia. Melbourne university RMIT earlier confirmed the pilot had studied there but left before completing his engineering qualification. According to Shamsi, interrogations of the 29-year-old pilot revealed he had been inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US in 2001. "The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the attorney-general was quoted as saying by the UAE's state news agency Wam on Friday. "During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks." The Wam report also said the pilot had told investigators "he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach". "He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim," Wam said. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported the man was issued an Australian student visa in 2014 and studied in the country in 2015-17, before leaving. This week, the Sydney Morning Herald unearthed tweets from al-Mammami's now-deleted X account in which he referred to his five years spent studying abroad in Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, as "the golden years of my religious commitment". More than 170 passengers and crew were on board flight FZ1073 on 30 September. In the days after the incident, Australian authorities confirmed they were looking into the man's links to Australia. The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - made up of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the country's security agency ASIO - said it was "investigating the man's links to Australia". Indian co-pilot Capt Smit Machchhar has been hailed a hero after managing to unlock the cockpit door while being violently attacked with an axe, allowing passengers to get in and take control of the aircraft. Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by Flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv. Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views. He was later hired by UAE-based Flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials. Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country. The man - who was piloting the aircraft - died on the scene, say emergency services. Israel said in September it would act in response to UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Casualties have been reported on the vessel, identified by a maritime intelligence firm as the oil and chemical tanker, Acers. The consulate, first established in 1838, was set to be closed by the Israeli government in retaliation for UK sanctions. The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for the remaining hostages held in Gaza. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
content: As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets. "There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school. "We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen." He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds. Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down. "They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population." The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis. The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country. Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter. The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system. The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them. On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million. But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them. Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem. It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages. When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils). "It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains. On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget. But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country. "It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest. "It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future." The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries. So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry. More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks. But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers. A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens. Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade. A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth. "For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether." Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests. But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests. "These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world." Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard. Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring. "Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better." The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise. More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country. But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape. The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant. Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration. Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race. Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks. Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth. He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history. Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration. "I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march. Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros. She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs. The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week. The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix. This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago. Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve. And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically. What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess. The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase. Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace. She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils. For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom. But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition. "In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris. "That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit." As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped. But not for long. A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street. "The canteen is still open." The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated. A second head teachers' union says it is "increasingly concerned" about members' "welfare and morale". St Martin's school is marking its recovery one year after it suffered extensive damage. Cheshire East's cabinet has agreed to launch a public consultation on removing the support. The pupils from Bicester have launched a petition to end adult content featuring school uniform. title: What happens when you grow up not knowing your family medical history?
content: When Aaliyah found a lump in her breast, she was anxious to find out if she had inherited an increased risk of cancer. But because she had been removed from her biological parents at the age of seven months and later adopted, she had no way of accessing her family medical history. "Not knowing anything about yourself genetically is terrifying," says the 26-year-old, "you can't even begin to imagine it." The lump turned out to be non-cancerous, but it was one of many occasions when she found herself unable to answer questions about her biological family's health. Aaliyah, now a trainee solicitor, spent years trying to source information from local authorities and eventually made an official data access request to Bradford Council, which removed her from her biological family as a baby. She says the whole process took its toll. "I would say bureaucratic hellscape is an understatement," she admits. Days before Aaliyah's 25th birthday, a large unmarked envelope landed on the doormat of her home, in Birmingham. "I rip it open, thinking it's an early birthday present," she says. But what was inside was the response to her data request - pages and pages of her family history, including some medical details she had been painstakingly trying to track down for years. The documents contained upsetting information alluding to the reason she was taken into care, alongside court records and a personal letter from her social worker. "They were just given to me in a completely nondescript pile, and they contained completely earth-shattering information, of which I don't think I have ever recovered from," she says. Aaliyah says knowing about her biological family's health could have helped her understand her own medical concerns. "My biological mother struggled with eating disorders all her life," she says. "I had very severe anorexia in my teens and that would have been incredibly useful to know." When a child is adopted in the UK, their NHS number - or equivalent health service identifier - is changed to protect their anonymity. Their existing medical records should be merged with their new record, but this does not necessarily include their wider family medical history. And while some local authorities offer specialist support for adoptees up to 21 or 25, the ease of access can vary across the country. The BBC contacted Bradford Council, which said: "We are genuinely sorry that when Aaliyah received sensitive and personal information through her subject access request, we did not offer the support or signposting she needed. We recognise that we should have done more. "Following Aaliyah's experience, we are strengthening our approach so that adults accessing their records are given clear information about the support available." Bradford Children and Families Trust has now offered Aaliyah a meeting to further discuss her experience. For Dr Chris Tennyson, a delay in getting information about his birth father's health could have put his life at risk. The 40-year-old clinical psychologist, from Belfast, was adopted as a baby in the 1980s to "a really loving mum and dad, [in a] really comfortable family home". But in his 20s, he became increasingly curious about his biological origins. He met his birth mother, but his attempts to find out about his father stalled after social workers warned him off asking questions. Eight years later, Chris tried to trace him again, but it wasn't until he was 33 that a meeting was finally arranged. Then, on the afternoon the father and son were due to meet, a social worker approached Chris. "There's something that I need to share with you," the social worker told him. "Your father wants me to let you know that there's a genetic medical condition within your family." A member of Chris's biological family died in 2000, when the condition came to light. At the time, other members of the family were offered testing. But Chris, who was then aged 14, was not contacted. The condition, called malignant hyperthermia, causes a potentially life-threatening reaction to certain drugs used during anaesthesia. While genes linked to it can run in families, not everyone who inherits one of these will necessarily experience a reaction with anaesthesia. After undergoing genetic tests, Chris discovered his potential risk at the age of 37 - some 23 years after the condition had become known in his wider family. He says a lack of understanding of how to support adopted adults resulted in the delay in him getting tested. Chris, who now works with adoption and fostering services in Northern Ireland, says the lack of available information for adoptees is "a huge blind spot". "There needs to be some kind of mechanism where adopted people's care records can be updated with family information that becomes available throughout the lifespan." First-time mum Courtney-Grace says she is relieved her baby daughter, Tine, will have access to the crucial family medical history she lacked when she grew up. Now living in the North of England, the 28-year-old was adopted as a baby and spent time in foster care as a teenager. "The only thing we knew about my medical history is my biological mom was mentally ill, and had depression." In her mid-20s, Courtney-Grace was diagnosed with a genetic mutation, which can be inherited and is associated with an increased risk of tumours. Her symptoms had previously been misdiagnosed as asthma and anxiety, which she says was based off the little doctors knew about her mum. Courtney-Grace believes allowing medical professionals access to familial history without interfering with data protection rules wouldn't just benefit adoptees, but the entire population. "The system needs a bit of an overhaul as a whole," she says. A government consultation on adoption support was launched in February 2026. Josh MacAlister, the minister for children and families - who is responsible for adoption and children's social care in England - told the BBC that medical records was one of the issues being looked at. "Adoption support and how it's set up at the moment isn't working well enough and there are obvious gaps in a number of areas that we're going to be looking at making changes to," MacAlister said. He acknowledged that the current system did not strike the right balance between safeguarding biological relatives' medical privacy and enabling adopted people to access information relevant to their own health. "We do need to change how we keep, retain, and share medical records," he said. Authorities in England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales all make provisions for adoptees to access their medical history, but the way this operates in practice can vary hugely in the different nations. None of the four nations gives patients the legal right to that information. But they advise that when a new clinical record is created for an adopted child, enough information must be kept to support continuity of care. NHS England said depending on the circumstances of an adoption there may be a need to "protect from disclosure any information about a third party". But it added that it is important any new NHS records, if created, contain sufficient information to allow for a continuity of care. For Courtney-Grace, her own diagnosis means her five-month-old daughter will now be closely monitored. Cord blood was collected when Tine was born, and it will be tested for the genetic condition when she is five. If she has inherited it, a plan will be put in place. "She has the medical information," Courtney-Grace says. "She can say, 'My mum has this'". A list of organisations in the UK offering support and information with some of the issues in this story is available at BBC Action Line Wellbeing champions at Wolverhampton and Worcester universities are helping students find support. A Gloucestershire man with terminal cancer shares the life lessons he wishes he'd learned sooner. One of Cornwall's MPs said he was "very hopeful" the plans would be scrapped permanently. Mental health is one of the "central drivers of absence" in secondary schools in Bristol, a council reports says. Nipsa has been holding meetings with members working across the health service and said they had given a clear message over their frustrations. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
content: Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children. Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks. But German police were already closing in on him. After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany. Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine". Both he and his country have denied any involvement. Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov. It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea. There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas. Both have been inoperable ever since. Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers. They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda. Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat. As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow. Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure. But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise. They went on following the forensic crumbs. Eventually they led to Ukraine. The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services. In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich. That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy. He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks. But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected. Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him. By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert. Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs. None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions. But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them. "Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that." Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe. That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it. Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution. "Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out. The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution. Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence. "At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained. Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned". Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far. Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August. He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation. Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him. Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning. He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver. But he is a civilian. Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him. In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war". As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more." Croatia is a different matter. The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg. After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop. It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv. It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone. When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that". This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further. "I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully. He argued that the Nord Stream pipelines had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed that to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe. "Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did." Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial. Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated. Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot. He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023. His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing. They are not saying, though. And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either. His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up. I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot. Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the tech firm admits customers may experience disruption to digital services due to the attacks. The charity came to national attention in October 2023 when Catherine visited the hub. Ukraine accused Russia of targeting two crowded vehicles in the front line city of Kramatorsk to kill as many civilians as possible. It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul. Ahead of a UK-EU summit next month, Burnham said he was committed to "see if we can bring the UK closer to Europe". Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Who is Nidal Hasan? What to know about US plans to livestream an execution online
content: The US Department of Defense plans to livestream on the internet the execution of a convicted killer, a move that has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum. Former US Army Major Nidal Hasan is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on 3 December. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said showing the killing online would act as a deterrent against future attacks. US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he approved of the plan but a determination still needed to be made. If it happens as planned, it would be the first-ever broadcast of a US execution. The decision to show the graphic death has led to condemnations and questions about legality. Nidal Hasan, a former US Army major and psychiatrist from Virginia, is due to be put to death on 3 December. John Galligan, a civilian lawyer advising Hasan, said that he was the first person to inform Hasan of the date of his sentence after seeing a social media post about it from the Pentagon's chief spokesman this week. Galligan told the BBC that the event is being treated like a "carnival" and is the "closest thing to a lynch mob mentality that we used to see in the olden days". Hasan, a native of Virginia, admitted to fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers in a crowded medical building on Fort Hood, a US military base in Texas, in 2009. He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair. The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. In addition to the 13 troops who died, 32 others were injured in the attack. It remains unclear whether any restrictions would be implemented on a livestream to limit who can watch the execution. Rules about how executions are carried out and who can watch vary by state, and the military also has its own rules. A number of states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many require journalists to be present. Some states allow the person being executed to invite people, and some allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses. Under US Army Regulation 190-55 which governs military executions, only certain categories of people, such as journalists and relatives, are permitted to be present. People aged under 18 are excluded. Critics of the plan to livestream Hasan's death say it will be hard, if not impossible, to prevent children from watching it live or in recordings afterwards. One survivor of the Fort Hood attack told the BBC that he opposed livestreaming the execution due to concerns about the message it might send to young people. Alonzo Lunsford, a former US Army sergeant who was shot seven times, said it should only be viewable by victims and their families. "As far as the families of the fallen and the families of the survivors, and the survivors themselves, yes, I think we should be able to look at it uncensored," he said. While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. The UN warned on Friday that livestreaming the execution would "constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment" that is banned under international law. UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said during Friday's press briefing in New York that the "possibility of…a government executing someone in public or in front of live cameras, frankly, is abhorrent". It's unclear how or where the US military plans to transmit the stream, and whether it would violate US laws or regulations. Legal challenges are expected in any case. Truth Social, the social media platform owned by President Trump, does not have a livestream video feature for users. The White House maintains official accounts and channels on the most widely used online platforms that are capable of streaming live video, namely Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X. All of the platforms have prohibitions in place on not only violent images and videos, but those that show death or otherwise glorify or make spectacle of violence. Meta - owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads - explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment. YouTube, owned by Google, bans all "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers", but says exceptions may be made for "content that is in the public interest". TikTok has a similar blanket ban. Its policy reads, "We don't allow extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing content—especially when it could cause viewers emotional distress." That includes the "moment of someone's death" and "the shooting of an individual". Two weeks ago, TikTok updated its policy to include a possible exception to the prohibition for graphic content that is in the "public interest". Several US states allow capital punishment to be carried out by firing squad, or by electrocution. Most executions are done by lethal injection of multiple drugs. Those drugs are now in short supply, however, due to concerns from drugmakers about how they are being used. The recent attempted execution of convicted killer Christa Pike in Tennessee failed for reasons that are still under investigation. Some have questioned the age of the drugs that were used. In the wake of Pike's failed execution, officials are now questioning what other methods may be available to kill condemned prisoners. The Pentagon announced on 5 October - five days after Pike's botched injections - that Hasan would die by firing squad. Trump approved of the plan, and said he also approved livestreaming the execution, but a final determination had not been made. Vice-President JD Vance, meanwhile, cast doubt that it would happen, saying he was not sure, and in any case, did not plan to watch. The last public execution in the US was the killing of Roscoe "Red" Jackson which took place in front of about 500 people inside a building Missouri, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks US executions. The most recent widely watched and notable one took place in Kentucky in 1936. Rainey Bethea, convicted of rape, was hanged in front of an outdoor audience estimated at around 20,000 people. Hasan's execution would be the first by the US military since 1961, and the first execution by firing squad since World War Two. A US Army private was hanged in 1961 after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. A young US Army deserter died by firing squad in January 1945 during the final months of WW2. With additional reporting from Kali Hays The planned execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years. Rules on the recording and filming of executions differ between state, federal and military regulations. Pete Hegseth says the execution will be public, but a legal expert says the "unprecedented" decision is on "uncertain legal terrain". Alonzo Lunsford tells the BBC the punishment befits the crime but he has some doubts whether the public should be able to watch it. title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago -  why are they resuming now?
content: They came in their thousands from near and far - men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow. It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heat wave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to the spectators. By the execution time of 5am, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000. That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70. The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream. Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner;" the local sheriff had died four months earlier, and his widow became the unlikely female replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death. That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in America. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky, and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later. By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now. A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan , who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas. The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad would be live-streamed. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked. "I never imagined [another] public execution," he told BBC. He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining; it was 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%. "It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said. It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's nearly certain that millions or more will tune in. With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment … bring your popcorn, invite your friends". Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream. "What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up … to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific." Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's 2002 death, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap. The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution. "I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific." But the polarisation and rhetoric in American politics may have, in some way, perhaps set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University. "Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't, and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution; they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'" Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong. Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said survey data points to a declining appetite for violence in the US. "This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labeled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people." "I think it's this: A public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country." Vice-President JD Vance, a Catholic, has said he would not be watching the execution . title: Ashe was too scared to cancel her wedding - the story became a hit song
content: No songwriter is ever off duty. And for the US pop singer Ashe, that included her wedding day. Last October, she was getting ready to tie the knot at a gorgeous hilltop ceremony in Nashville when inspiration struck. As she watched her family gather, the musician flashed back to her first wedding, almost a decade earlier. The contrast was stark. She's called that first marriage "horrifying". Her ex, who she met in college, was, she says, emotionally manipulative and psychologically abusive. He had insisted on a beachfront wedding, which sounds romantic until you learn that Ashe has a fear of the ocean. In the run-up, she had been tempted to call it off, but felt powerless to stand up for herself. On her second wedding day, she realised the opposite was true. "I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life," says the singer, now in her early 30s. "I thought, if this didn't feel right, I could totally put a halt to the whole thing. I definitely didn't have that first time around." As she adjusted her veil and prepared to walk down the aisle, she filed that feeling away. Two months later, and back at work, the idea resurfaced and a song spilled out. Its name? Stop the Wedding. It unfolds like a movie scene. Ashe pleads with her younger self to trust her instincts. "You know how you really feel / You don't have to waste your life," she sings, as the wedding band stutters to an uncertain halt. "Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 per cent," Ashe says. "If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner. Maybe not at the altar. Maybe weeks before – but it was something I really could have used." What about the line where she pledges to "burn the wedding dress and run away"? "I didn't burn my dress," she laughs, "but I did get into a bathtub with it for a photoshoot right after I left my ex-husband, which really ruined it!" Released in August, Stop The Wedding this week became one of the 10 most-played songs in the world on Spotify. On Friday, it broke into the top five of the UK singles chart, while on TikTok, thousands of videos use Ashe's song to highlight red flags in their own relationships. "I don't think I even let myself dream of this," she says of the song's popularity. "It's something you hope for when you're first starting out, but when you've been in the business for 10 years, it's a little bit of a shock to the system." The success is even sweeter because, three years ago, Ashe nearly quit music altogether. A native of San Jose, she grew up in a conservative household where the radio was permanently tuned to Christian stations. It was her grandad who introduced her to rock music, playing Tom Petty and Bob Dylan on long road trips. By her teens, she was writing her own music. After studying orchestral composition at Boston's Berklee College of Music, she moved to Nashville and quickly found work as a songwriter. She scored an early credit on Demi Lovato's 2017 song You Don't Do It For Me Anymore; but slowly grew frustrated that other people were singing her words. The decision to become Ashe, whose full name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, didn't happen overnight. She appeared as a featured vocalist on a handful of dance tracks before plunging into a solo career. Her then-husband was not impressed. "I remember him saying, '[After this] no-one's ever going to love you for you. Anyone you meet now is going to meet you as Ashe, and I met you before'. "It was truly manipulative, and it kept me stuck. It kept me stuck for a long, long time." It can't be a coincidence that a song she wrote after signing her divorce papers became her breakthrough hit. Moral of The Story (key lyric: " you can think that you're in love / when you're really just in pain ") was released in 2019, and hit one billion streams after appearing in the hit Netflix series To All the Boys: PS I Still Love You. Ashe was suddenly playing bigger venues and duetting with Niall Horan, but work became all consuming. When her brother died of an overdose in 2020, she was back on stage within a month. "There was so much momentum and I was saying yes to far too many things," she reflects now. "It got to a point where the idea of touring was giving me panic attacks, and I just couldn't stomach being Ashe, which is such a shame, because I'm her." In 2023, she had a nervous breakdown and stepped away from showbusiness. "I had to halt everything. I bought a house in Nashville, I gardened, I saw a therapist and I gave myself a chance to miss music." For six months, she led a quiet, domestic life. But when pop singer Suki Waterhouse invited her to a session, it rekindled her passion for writing. She made a tentative return with 2024's deeply confessional album Wilson, then teamed up with Billie Eilish's brother Finneas O'Connell to form The Favors, before signing a new deal with Atlantic Records. Those experiences mean she's treating the success of Stop The Wedding very differently. "You can get swept up by all the updates on your phone, but this time I'm navigating the emotions of that, and also going for a four-mile walk and calling my mom. "There's a real groundedness." The same can't be said for her new album, Girl of Your Dreams, which is almost deliriously over the top. Stop The Wedding sets the tone, with abrupt tempo changes that track Ashe's inner turmoil. Lasso The Moon is more whimsical, setting out the star's outlandish requirements for a new partner. "God forbid I raise my standards," she laughs. Love Bomb explores the psychology of a manipulative ex (guess who?); while Swan Lake is a comically villainous portrait of Ashe's possessiveness, complete with a Bugsy Malone chorus line. It's a deliberately maximalist record, recalling the lush orchestrations of ELO and The Carpenters, with a nod to the revivalist pop of Ashe's friend Laufey. "We were so bored of making music that's boring," she says. "It scratches an itch for me as an artist to do something different and not meet the status quo." The album ends back at her second wedding. The closing track focuses on the "real, true, constant love" she's found with musician John Clark Canada. "You'll be my Tuesday night and my Sunday drive / And the last speech at my funeral," she sings. Expanding on that idea, Ashe incorporates the ebullient sound of a New Orleans funeral band in the song's closing moments. And the person they're burying is the disillusioned girl from Stop The Wedding. Ashe's album, Girl of Your Dreams, is out on 16 October.
