title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
content: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law. Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines. The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes. He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines". "[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence. Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others. However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals. title: Two Renoir paintings stolen from French museum are recovered
content: Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said. The two works were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the French impressionist had lived during his final years. The local mayor praised authorities for recovering the paintings and said the news gave immense joy and profound relief. Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum, the town hall confirmed in a statement. The theft was the latest in a series of high-profile art heists in Europe. The two missing paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886). The thieves had used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings inside the museum and had initially made off with four paintings, but dropped two of them in the museum's garden as they fled "These two paintings are far more than works of art. They are part of our city's history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer," said Mayor Bryan Masson, who is part of France's National Rally. The town hall said initially that it would provide further details of the recovery on Friday, but cancelled a planned press conference. The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks. Opened in 1960, it houses a variety of objects that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters. Earlier this year paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum near the Italian city of Parma, in a raid that lasted just three minutes. They were recovered in August. France saw its biggest art robbery in years last October, when crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris. Disguised as construction workers, the thieves broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours. They used an angle-grinder to open display cases and made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to France's 19th-Century queens and empresses. The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security. The motorcycle will be telling the story of racer George Brown at the place where he made history. title: Man named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
content: A man named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has secured a narrow victory in Peru's local elections, exit polls show. The candidate for the centre-left Ahora Nación party was elected mayor of Queropalca, a remote district in the Peruvian Andes. Some 229 residents voted for the 45-year-old, putting him ahead of the second-place candidate from right-wing Renovación Popular Perú by just 25 votes. Despite being elected to represent fewer than 1,000 people, his forenames being those of two notorious fascist dictators has drawn outsized international attention to the small corner of the country. Data from Peru's elections office showed a little over 700 people had participated in the election, with Simeon securing around 34% of the vote. He was born in the district in the central department of Huánuco, some 360km (224 miles) from the capital, Lima, according to his candidate profile. That he shares his name with Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini - "two of the most well-known figures of 20th-Century European totalitarian regimes" - has made his candidacy a "striking event", local outlet Peru21 reported. Despite the curiosity generated by his name, local media noted that Hitler Guesclin Alba Sánchez had been elected mayor of Yúngar in 2018. He reportedly beat rival candidate Lenin Vladimir Rodríguez Valverde after campaigning on the slogan "I'm the good Hitler". A politician named Adolf Hitler Uunona attracted similar attention in 2020 after winning local elections in Namibia - a former German colony where Adolf and other Germanic first names are not uncommon. title: Three Saudi nationals killed in Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport
content: Three Saudi Arabian nationals have been killed in two attacks on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, the country's civil aviation authority has said, after Yemen's Houthis said they had targeted the facility. The attacks also resulted in "injuries to a number of Saudi citizens and residents of various nationalities", the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement on X. It added that the first attack on Thursday targeted the airport while the second had struck an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia. One of its pilots was among those killed, the airline said in a statement. Air traffic had returned to normal, the civil aviation authority said. Yemen's Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked the airport with two ballistic missiles. The Iran-aligned group said it had also targeted an airport in Najran city near the Saudi border with Yemen, and Khamis Mushait air base further north. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed these attacks. The latest casualties follow the deaths of three people in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October. Two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, the civil aviation body said on Wednesday. Another person was killed at King Khalid airport in Riyadh. The latest attacks come amid a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west. The Houthi military spokesman said the previous two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" that saw "60 air strikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours". The group says it is targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war. The conflict has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive. That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. But Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government. A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. But the informal ceasefire began to unravel in July. The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they say is a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport. The families allege that men with links to the Saudi government helped those who carried out the 2001 attacks, something the country denies. title: Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest
content: Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday. The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists. The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on calls for his resignation. The protest comes just months after the movement brought thousands of young people onto Delhi's streets in July, in demonstrations that saw violent clashes with police and forced India's education minister to resign. Police say they have denied permission for Saturday's gathering, and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed off with huge metal barricades. The restrictions have caused major disruption across central Delhi, with traffic diverted from several key roads. A journey that would normally take 15 minutes took more than an hour this morning. At Jantar Mantar, police and paramilitary personnel are stationed behind barricades and ropes, preventing people from entering the protest site. Drones could be seen flying overhead. Some protesters who arrived early were stopped and questioned by security personnel. The BBC also saw at least five people being detained near the site. Journalists covering the protest have been cordoned off into a designated area nearby. At a nearby roundabout, loudspeakers repeatedly broadcast appeals for people to cooperate with the police. Delhi Police has defended the measures, saying they were necessary to maintain public safety and prevent overcrowding at Jantar Mantar, which can accommodate only 1,000 people at a time. Several trains to Delhi have also been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering. But Abhijeet Dipke, founder ⁠of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may". "If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing ​Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X. The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations demanding education reforms over the summer. The resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July was seen as a major victory for the group. CJP protesters returned to the streets last week with a rally in Mumbai to demand Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held another large rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore). Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days. Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups. CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi. In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests. Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP. "Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said. Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them. "In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied." The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather. At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year. The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list. But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations. The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission. For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue. Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media. It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul. title: We sold everything and bought a one-way ticket to take our three children travelling
content: Dani and Tom Wooldridge worked hard to transform a 1970s house into a beloved family home after they bought it about seven years ago. Dani, 39, a nurse, also ran an aesthetics business while Tom, 38, had a construction business. Three children, a close extended family and lots of friends. A happy life. Yet in May this year, the five of them sold their possessions and home, and bought a one-way ticket heading for Indonesia, with the only things they owned in the world now stowed in backpacks in the luggage compartment. With Olivia, 12, Morgan, seven, and four-year-old George, the Woolridges are planning to travel the world, with no endpoint in sight, hoping to see every continent. Five months in, over a video call from the Indonesian island of Lombok, Dani and Tom explain the decisions which have brought them to the shores of south-east Asia. Both of them had gone travelling for a period of time in their early 20s, a classic gap-year style experience, and had enjoyed taking holidays, particularly to sunny destinations. Dani said: "It was always a conversation we had but once you start having kids and you've got the mortgage and everything like that it's kind of, 'oh it's not the right time'." But nearly two years ago, the family took a holiday to Thailand over Christmas. "We were fortunate enough to have a month over there, travelled round with the kids and obviously they were almost two years younger than they are now, and managed really well. Tom added: "It all went really smoothly and it was great seeing the kids experience a completely different world to what we'd all grown up. It just felt so great exploring with them. Dani said that sparked their interest to start researching and meeting other families who had decided to jet off. "We made lots of lists - lots of positives, lots of negatives," she said. "Can we do this? How are we still going to educate our children? We had a home, we had our businesses, we had careers. What do we do about all that?" Once they made the decision, they knew they had to be "100% committed". Dani thought at first they should rent their house out "so we've got something to come back to" but Tom wanted to sell, and the couple realised they didn't want to leave the responsibility of managing it to people back home. The boys were excited about the idea from the start but the couple admit it was harder for their daughter. Tom said: "Olivia was a bit nervous. She'd just started high school in the September and we left in May. She was very apprehensive about leaving all her friends. "Morgan and George do mention their friends now and again, but they're a bit younger so they didn't have that emotional attachment as much as Olivia." When they told their parents about their plans, their initial reaction was "why are you selling everything you've worked so hard to get?" "Most people have got bets on when we're coming back," Dani said, laughing. Tom added: "They've all got a year each." After selling their house at the start of the year, they lived in rented accommodation for a number of months, before heading to the airport in May for the big farewell. Leaving was "very emotional", Dani said. "We were very fortunate that we had a lot of family coming to the airport with us," added Tom. "We'd checked our luggage in and we got to the security gates - that was hard. "We were so fortunate to have a close family and friendship group as well. They're the people we miss and that's what we miss from back home, the people that were in our lives. Not so much the material things we had." However once the plane had taken off and the goodbyes were behind them, the excitement started to kick in. "We remembered where we were going," joked Tom. Even though they had both been to their first destination, Bali in Indonesia, before, the culture shock still hit them. "It's just everything. Your senses are just heightened. It's the smells, seeing everything around, it's so different to home. "We went to Bali 15 years ago when it was a lot quieter," added Dani. "People have said how busy it is now, and it was. "The first day or two was very overwhelming. Our daughter was still a bit emotional. She was up and down with things and we were all a bit jet lagged. "We went to Uluwatu first and it has got so busy. Even us walking down a road, I was nervous. Scooters everywhere." But there were also upsides, Tom said. "The food instantly was amazing. And the people are just beautiful, and so kind. And just to feel the heat on our skin." They moved to different parts of the island, swapping the beaches in the south to climb the volcanic Mount Batur in the north, and spending time in the cultural village of Ubud inland. They then went island hopping eastwards across the Indonesian archipelago before doubling back to Lombok for a second stay. "We were moving around quite a bit," Dani said. "So each time it was almost like that feeling of going home because we were packing up, but we weren't going home. I think it took us months to really think, 'wow, we're not actually going home'." Leaving the UK behind has not meant abandoning education, Dani stressed. "Even though we want our children to experience the world and have that kind of real world learning, we have said we also want them to have opportunities. So if they want to go to university and be a doctor or a nurse or whatever career path they want to go down, we still want them to have those opportunities," she added. They have a "huge bag" full of textbooks and workbooks recommended by teachers before they left and they are following the UK teaching curriculum. Olivia has an online maths tutor, who was previously head of maths at her high school in Rhondda Cynon Taf, and had also taught Tom at the same school. The boys have a tutor who covers the primary curriculum with them and does English and some science with Olivia. Although the big downside to their journey is missing time with family back home, Dani and Tom say the cultural experiences and confidence the children have already gained from their travels, meeting such a wide variety of people and having the opportunity to live such an outdoor life, outweighs the negatives. The family is due to be moving on to Malaysia after spending five months travelling around Indonesia, most recently in Lombok for a second stint, where the children have been attending a world schooling centre - which the couple described as a "lovely routine" with amazing friends. After bringing "way too much stuff" with them initially, they have given away possessions to locals they have met along their travels and refined it down to two large 120-litre backpacks for the parents and two 100-litre rolling packs including one filled with educational materials. "The kids will have virtually nothing on their backs, just maybe a really small backpack to get on the plane," said Tom. "We thought the kids would be excited at carrying their backpacks. Yeah, they're not onboard with that," laughed Dani. Among the things they have planned for Malaysia is visiting an orangutang sanctuary in Borneo and another longer stop at a world schooling centre to give the children more chances to spend time with peers. Then they move into Thailand, where both Dani's mum and Tom's parents will make separate visits and after figuring out a good location to celebrate Dani's 40th birthday, will move through Cambodia, Vietnam and the Philippines. With all that, they have the next year "roughly" planned out. They have allowed for contingencies and emergencies - Tom has already had to fly home once for a funeral - but don't have a firm destination in mind yet once they leave Asia, barring a likely brief visit home to catch up with family. "We're going to do as much as we feel we want to in a continent and then go to the next one," explained Tom. "Just keep going for as long as we can, and want to. If at some point we don't want to then we'll have explored a lot of places to pick somewhere to stop." It is, in many respects, the bucket list to end all bucket lists. But if they had to put one destination at the top, what would it be? For Dani, it's to go on an African safari. "I've always wanted to see Africa and I've never been. That's always been on my list." Tom says: "Tahiti is coming to my head. That's with my surfing background. The place looks beautiful. And we will be going there. I'm 40 next December so..."
